recipe.history:
Cayenne pepper — named after the capital city of French Guiana on the northeastern coast of South America — is one of the oldest cultivated spices in the Western Hemisphere. Its origins trace back at least 7,000 years to the indigenous peoples of Central and South America, particularly the Tupi-Guaraní cultures who domesticated Capsicum annuum long before European contact. When Christopher Columbus encountered the fiery red fruits in 1492, he mistakenly called them peppers in a nod to the familiar black pepper he had set out to find, and the misnomer stuck. The Aztecs and Mayans had already been using cayenne not only as food and seasoning but as medicine, insect repellent, and even a form of warfare — blowing powdered chili into the eyes of enemies. Spanish and Portuguese traders carried cayenne back across the Atlantic, seeding its cultivation across Africa, India, and Southeast Asia, where it became so thoroughly adopted that many cultures now consider it a native ingredient.

Cayenne's arrival in American cuisine was gradual but inevitable. The spice traveled into the cuisine of the American South through Caribbean and West African culinary traditions carried by enslaved people, fusing with French Creole and Cajun cooking to create the fiery, soulful flavor profiles of Louisiana and the Gulf Coast. By the 19th century, cayenne was a pantry staple from New Orleans to the Texas frontier. Its entry into the burger world came naturally: American cooks discovered that a pinch of cayenne in a beef patty or mixed into a sauce could cut through the richness of fat, sharpen the umami, and leave a slow, satisfying heat that lingered on the back of the palate. Burger joints from roadside diners to upscale gastropubs began reaching for cayenne as a secret weapon — subtly present but impossible to ignore, the kind of heat that keeps you coming back for another bite rather than reaching for a glass of water.

I remember the first time a burger made me sweat and smile at the same time. I was nineteen, sitting on a cracked vinyl stool at a lunch counter in Albuquerque that smelled like cast iron and decades of rendered fat. The cook — a stout man with a salt-and-pepper mustache — slapped a patty onto the flat-top without ceremony, and within seconds the whole place filled with the warm, smoky bite of cayenne blooming in the beef's own fat. When the burger arrived wrapped in wax paper, the first bite sent a slow fire spreading across my lips that didn't ache — it glowed. It felt earned. There was something honest about that heat, nothing masked or apologetic about it. That burger told me exactly what it was, and it made no concessions. I have been chasing that precise, unapologetic warmth in every cayenne burger I've eaten or cooked since, and the Yes I Cayenne Burger is my closest attempt to bottle that afternoon in New Mexico.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a burger patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the point at which the proteins have set just enough to hold the patty together while leaving the interior a rosy, almost magenta pink, swimming in its own juices. Cooking a burger beyond this point is an act of culinary surrender — well-done beef loses the fat-soluble flavors that make ground chuck worth eating, becoming dry, grey, and texturally indistinguishable from a hockey puck. The Maillard crust developed on a screaming-hot cast iron pan or grill provides all the cooked, caramelized complexity you need on the outside; the inside should remain a tender, yielding contrast. Medium rare is not a preference — it is a philosophy grounded in the chemistry of meat. It respects the animal, the butcher, and the diner. Every degree above 135°F is a degree of flavor sacrificed for nothing more than unfounded anxiety. Cook your burgers medium rare, rest them briefly, and serve them immediately. There is no other way.
ingredients: 500g (1 lb 2 oz) ground beef chuck, 80/20 fat ratio
1 tsp neutral oil (such as canola, for cooking)
300g (2 1/3 cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 small garlic clove, minced to a paste
1/2 red onion, very thinly sliced into rings
Bread and butter pickle chips (8–10 slices)
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: In the bowl of a stand mixer, combine bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add 2 eggs and the warm milk. Mix with the dough hook on low until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.

2. Increase mixer speed to medium and add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. Continue kneading for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly away from the bowl sides.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, approximately 1.5 to 2 hours.

4. Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 130g each). Shape each into a tight ball by tucking the dough underneath itself. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let proof for 45–60 minutes until puffy and nearly doubled.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make egg wash. Gently brush the tops of the buns, then sprinkle with sesame seeds.
6. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.
7. Make the cayenne aioli: In a medium bowl, whisk together egg yolks, Dijon mustard, lemon juice, apple cider vinegar, garlic paste, cayenne, and smoked paprika until combined.

8. Combine the neutral oil and olive oil in a measuring cup with a pour spout. While whisking constantly, add the oil in an extremely slow, thin drizzle — almost drop by drop at first — until the mixture begins to emulsify and thicken. Once it has clearly thickened and emulsified (about halfway through the oil), you can pour the remainder in a thin, steady stream, whisking continuously.
9. Season the aioli with salt to taste. Cover and refrigerate until needed. The aioli will keep for up to 3 days.

10. Cook the bacon: Lay bacon strips in a cold cast iron or heavy skillet. Set heat to medium. Cook, turning occasionally, until fat is rendered and bacon is crispy, about 8–10 minutes. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate and set aside. Pour off all but 1 tsp of bacon fat from the pan.

11. Prepare the patties: Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. In a large bowl, gently combine the beef with cayenne, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, kosher salt, and black pepper. Mix with your hands just until the spices are evenly distributed — do not overwork the meat.

12. Divide into 2 equal portions (approximately 250g each). Form each into a patty roughly 4.5 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Refrigerate uncovered for 10 minutes to firm up.
13. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until it begins to faintly smoke. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place the patties dimple-side-up in the pan. Do not press, move, or disturb them.

14. Sear for 2.5–3 minutes until a deep mahogany crust has formed on the bottom. Flip once. Add the butter to the pan and, as it foams, tilt the pan slightly and baste the tops of the patties with the butter using a spoon.

15. Cook for a further 1.5–2 minutes on the second side. Begin checking the internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Pull the patties from the heat at 130°F / 54°C — they will carry-over cook to 133–135°F / 56–57°C while resting. This is medium rare. It is the only acceptable outcome.
16. Immediately lay a slice of pepper jack cheese on each patty. Tent loosely with foil and rest for 3 minutes. Do not skip the rest — this allows the juices to redistribute.
17. While the patties rest, slice the brioche buns in half and place cut-side-down in the residual fat in the pan over medium heat. Toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped.

18. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous tablespoon of cayenne aioli on both the top and bottom bun. On the bottom bun, layer: butter lettuce, tomato slices (seasoned with a pinch of flaky salt), the cheese-topped patty, bacon strips, red onion rings, and pickle chips.
19. Finish with an additional small drizzle of cayenne aioli directly onto the patty if desired. Cap with the top bun, press gently, and serve immediately.
